units.text: EXT. ROOFTOP PIGEON LOFT - EVENING
Above the chimney pots, a plywood loft leans against the wind.
Copper light spills over tar paper and laundry lines.
OLD ANSELMO CRUZ-BELLAMY (70s) kneels at the loft door, palms open.
Beside him, his granddaughter NIMA (9) holds a single grey bird against her chest.
She has been quiet all day.
Now she squeezes, and the bird beats its wings once, hard, against her ribs.
Grandpa, it's scared.
units.name: NIMA

units.text: It is.
units.name: ANSELMO

units.text: He does not take it from her.
His hands hover, trembling, close enough to catch, far enough to let her choose.
She opens her fingers a little.
Then a little more.
The bird sits in the cradle of her palm, small heart drumming.
If I let go, it won't come back.
units.name: NIMA

units.text: Maybe.
units.name: ANSELMO

units.text: You said they always come back.
units.name: NIMA

units.text: I said they come home. It's not the same as coming back to us.
units.name: ANSELMO

units.text: She considers this with the gravity of the very young.
The wind lifts her hair across her eyes.
Her arms shoot up.
The bird explodes out of her hands, a clap of feathers, and is a speck, then a rumor, then gone over the river.
She stares at her empty palms.
He stares at her.
Slowly, she leans into his shoulder, and he lets out the breath he has held since April.
